draft.title: Reading a climate graph
card: A climate graph shows the average climate of one place over a year. The months run along the bottom.
show the average rainfall for each month. Read their height against the rainfall scale, usually in millimetres.
shows the average temperature for each month. Read it against the temperature scale, usually in degrees Celsius.
Months with tall columns are the wet season. Months with short columns are the dry season. Where the line is high it is hot, and where it is low it is cool.
draft.remember: Columns show rainfall, the line shows temperature, and both are monthly averages.

a.q: On a climate graph for a town, the columns are tallest in January and shortest in July. What does this show?
opts: January is the wettest month and July is the driest
January is the hottest month and July is the coolest
January is the driest month and July is the wettest
January has the most sunshine and July the least
a.why: Columns show average rainfall, so tall columns mean a wet month and short columns mean a dry month. The temperature is shown by the line, not the columns, so the hottest and coolest months cannot be read from column height.
a.clue: Which part of the graph do the columns show?

b.q: A climate graph for Darwin shows columns that are very tall from December to March and very short from June to August. The line stays high all year. Which description fits?
opts: A hot place with a wet summer and a dry winter
A hot place with a dry summer and a wet winter
A cool place with a wet summer and a dry winter
A place with a wet summer and a cool winter
b.why: Tall columns from December to March show a wet season in the Australian summer, and short columns from June to August show a dry winter. The line stays high, so it is hot all year. A cool winter would need the line to drop, and it does not.
b.clue: Read the columns for rain and the line for temperature, one at a time.

a.best: January is the wettest month and July is the driest

b.best: A hot place with a wet summer and a dry winter
